transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 58m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Ethan (CTO, Monarch), Priya (Platform Lead), Luis (SRE), Alma (Security)

Summary:
Monarch Robotics is evaluating Redwood for inference serving for their fleet-management and QA automation models. Primary concerns: cross-region latency (APAC + EU heavy), data residency for EU customers, fallbacks when a region loses capacity, and suitability of Private deployment versus Hosted/Dedicated. They requested concrete latency/cost tradeoffs, onboarding steps for a VPC-private install, and an operations playbook for graceful degradation.

Topics discussed:
- Current traffic profile and performance targets (p95 < 200ms for short prompts; bulk batch jobs tolerance)
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (latency, data egress, SLA)
- Multi-region routing, sticky sessions, and KV cache priming implications
- Failover policies: dual-write vs active-active vs passive failover
- Security controls (SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs), and regulatory residency
- Pilot scope and next steps

Action items (summarized above).

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Um, quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE on Redwood inference, and Sofia's our SE. Do folks want to do quick intros?
[00:06] Ethan: Yeah hi, Ethan Cole here, CTO at Monarch. We manage the orchestration for the fleet of warehouse robots; a lot of our inferencing is at the edge but we do heavier tasks in the cloud.
[00:13] Priya: Priya — platform lead. I'm owning the integration of model endpoints into our svc mesh.
[00:16] Luis: Luis, SRE — I'll be running the rollout and oncall.
[00:19] Alma: Alma, security — looking at compliance and data flow.
[00:22] Jordan: Great, thanks. So high level what we're hoping to cover: where you're at today, what constraints (latency, cost, residency), and then tradeoffs across our Hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private VPC/on-prem options.

[00:40] Priya: To frame it, we've got about 3 model classes: short decision prompts (50–150 tokens) — real-time for fleet routing, medium dialog-ish prompts (up to 512 tokens) for QA, and batch telemetry embeddings. The real-time stuff is sensitive at p95. We want to keep it under 200 ms ideally in EU and APAC.
[01:02] Sofia: Cool. That sounds like a mix where latency SLOs will drive placement. Quick question — are your edge devices talking directly to Redwoods hosted endpoints or via regional gateways?
[01:12] Ethan: Right now we proxy through regional gateways in GCP/EU and a cluster in Singapore. So traffic flows to nearest gateway then to a central inferencing pool.
[01:20] Jordan: Got it. Two immediate patterns we typically recommend: 1) Hosted with regional steering — use Redwood's smart routing to send to nearest region and use smaller model variants there; 2) Dedicated pools pinned to regions for predictable tail latency. Private is usually chosen when data residency or network isolation is mandated.

[01:45] Luis: Explain the routing failover — if APAC region hits capacity, what happens to real-time requests? We can't see spike-induced tail latencies for robots.
[01:55] Sofia: Sure. Our smart routing has policy-based fallback: first try preferred region, then failover to a warm regional pool (another region's dedicated or hosted variant) depending on policy. There's an option for active-active with traffic split which keeps latencies optimal but requires cross-region state for KV cache priming. If you do passive failover, you'll see cold-start KV misses and an initial latency penalty.
[02:22] Priya: Cold KV misses — can you quantify? Like how many ms?
[02:25] Sofia: It varies a lot by model size and sequence length. For a 512-token dialog on A100-class instance with warm KV, p95 delta might be 30–80ms. Cold KV where cache hasn't been primed can add 120–400ms on first few tokens, depending on batch and quantization.
[02:42] Ethan: That's significant for real-time. Could we do sticky sessions to keep robot sessions routing to same region?
[02:46] Jordan: Yes, session-affinity is supported. The tradeoff is you need to ensure the origin region has sufficient capacity or implement a circuit-breaker fallback that routes to a lower-cost or lower-latency model variant.

[03:05] Alma: From security/residency perspective: If we use Hosted but route EU traffic to EU region, is data ever egressed out of EU for processing or logs?
[03:12] Sofia: With Hosted, you can pin processing to region; logs and observability data are retained per-region depending on plan. For enterprise plans we offer region data residency controls and can integrate with your KMS for envelope encryption. For strict residency we recommend Private.
[03:28] Alma: Private means we run Redwood control plane in our VPC? Or is it a hybrid? What's the connectivity pattern?
[03:33] Sofia: Private deployments have a customer-managed control plane option: you host the control plane components in your VPC and we provide the inference runtime as containers you can run in your cluster or we can deploy a managed appliance. Connectivity is through VPC peering or private link; audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[03:49] Luis: Operationally, how long does onboarding take for private? We can't have months of blocked infra work.
[03:55] Jordan: Typical time ranges: Dedicated reserved capacity (hosted) — 1–2 weeks for provisioning and baseline testing; Private VPC install — 4–8 weeks end-to-end depending on approvals and network changes. We have an onboarding checklist Sofia will share that lists required networking changes and KMS steps.

[04:15] Priya: For the Dedicated option, what's the SLA and the bumping rules if we exceed capacity?
[04:20] Jordan: Dedicated is SLA-backed; we'll commit to throughput/latency targets for the provisioned pool. For bursts, we support configurable autoscale or burst capacity against a shared pool, but that affects latency guarantees. Canary rollouts and fallback to hosted can also be part of the policy.

[04:35] Ethan: For our economics — we're sensitive to token cost and also to persistent GPU reservation cost. If Dedicated means always-on GPUs and we underutilize, it might be costly. How do you recommend modeling that?
[04:44] Sofia: We usually model expected QPS and sequence length, then estimate token rates and CPU/GPU utilization. Redwood Optimize suggests batching and quantization profiles; with continuous batching you can reduce tokens per dollar. We'll send a spreadsheet template so you can plug in your QPS.

[05:05] Priya: One tricky bit — our QA tooling sometimes reruns prompts for auditing and we store conversation logs for 30 days. Any suggestions to reduce egress risk while storing logs?
[05:14] Alma: And we need to ensure logs with EU PII don't leave EU.
[05:17] Sofia: On Hosted you can use regional log retention; for sensitive PII we recommend encrypting logs with your KMS and consider Private if you want complete control over storage endpoints. Also redact PII at the application layer before sending to inference if feasible.

[05:32] Luis: Let's talk about incident scenarios. Suppose a whole region becomes unavailable for 15 minutes during peak — what's the recommended SLO posture?
[05:39] Jordan: We recommend defining SLOs by feature: for critical real-time routing, set an SLO that tolerates partial degradation for up to X minutes with defined fallback model behavior. For Monarch I'd expect something like: 99% availability for critical real-time endpoints with graceful degradation to lower-fidelity model variants under sustained region failure.
[06:00] Sofia: Tech options: active-active across two regions with cross-region KV replication reduces cold-start but adds cost and complexity. Alternatively, keep one warm regional replica and a fast fallback path that returns a cached response or simplified deterministic policy for a limited window.
[06:14] Ethan: Cross-region KV replication — is it supported out of the box? There's concern about consistency and egress.
[06:19] Sofia: It's supported as an enterprise feature in Dedicated/Private setups. We provide async replication with eventual consistency; replication bandwidth and residency needs to be configured to meet your compliance needs. If you need strict residency, cross-region replication might be off the table.
[06:34] Priya: How do you instrument the system to alert us before a region is exhausted?
[06:37] Sofia: Redwood Console provides per-model token-level metrics, queue depth, and latency tails. You can set alerting on p95/p99 and auto-trigger routing policies or autoscale. We can integrate with PagerDuty and your existing metrics via exporters.

[06:55] Luis: Regarding traffic steering: is the routing policy deterministic (e.g., by prefix or IP) or can it be dynamic based on load and p95 targets?
[07:02] Jordan: Both. You can define static affinity rules or dynamic policies that evaluate region latency/capacity and route accordingly. We also support header- or token-based routing for session stickiness.

[07:18] Alma: A question from legal: for Private deployment, what audit artifacts do you provide for SOC2/ISO traceability?
[07:24] Sofia: For Private, you control log retention but we provide structured audit logs for admin actions, model version changes, and key events. We can include standard audit schemas and a playbook for evidence collection — we'll include sample artifacts in the doc pack.

[07:40] Ethan: Ok, practical ask — can you run a short benchmark for our 512-token dialog model from APAC to EU to NA and show p50/p95 for hosted vs dedicated?
[07:48] Jordan: Yes, we can. For a benchmark we'll need an anonymized prompt set and expected QPS. If you can provide a 2-hour window for a live test, we can stand up a dedicated pool and run measurements.

[07:59] Priya: We'll need the test to simulate our gateway routing so results are similar to production.
[08:03] Sofia: We'll work with you on traffic shaping. Also note that for Hosted, noisy neighbors can cause variance; Dedicated isolates capacity so p95 is more stable.

[08:15] Luis: One more — how does graceful degradation surface to the client SDK? Do you get structured error codes or is the response content downgraded?
[08:21] Sofia: We return structured status codes and model metadata. For degradations we can return a sentinel header indicating a fallthrough to a lower-fidelity model and an explanation payload. You can then decide to retry, degrade UI, or show cached content.

[08:38] Jordan: To recap quickly: we'll send the hosted vs dedicated cost/latency spreadsheet, Sofia will share private deployment checklist and network diagram, we'll propose dates for a 90-minute technical deep dive and a live benchmark window. Also we flagged residency constraints that might force Private for certain EU customers.

[08:56] Ethan: Sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood side we should be aware of?
[09:00] Sofia: Nothing immediate. For Private we'll need your infra contacts for peering and KMS access, and a security questionnaire will follow.

[09:08] Priya: Alright, we'll get those items together. Thanks, this was helpful.
[09:13] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with the materials and a proposed schedule.

[09:20] (call ends)
